GPS works like a one‑way radio broadcast, not a two‑way network. Each of the ~30 MEO satellites continuously transmits a low‑power, spread‑spectrum signal on several frequencies. Every satellite uses a unique pseudo‑random code (PRN) so that many receivers can lock onto the same signal at the same time without interfering with each other—think of it as a radio station that anyone can tune into.

A GPS receiver only needs to hear **at least four** of those signals to compute its position, velocity and time. Because the satellites are always transmitting, the number of users has virtually no impact on the system’s capacity; the “handful” of satellites simply broadcast, and millions of devices independently listen and decode the data. This passive, code‑division multiple‑access design lets a small constellation serve the entire world.

| **Signal structure (pseudo‑random codes, error‑correcting codes)** | Strong codes let many receivers share the same frequency (CDMA) without interference, but longer codes increase acquisition time for weak receivers. |
